captions.instagram:
How does a computer work?

A computer is billions of switches following a list of tiny instructions, one clock tick at a time. Take a desktop apart, type your name and see its bytes, and step a real 8-bit CPU through fetch, decode and execute.

→ Every computer has the same few parts: a processor, memory, storage, graphics and power.
→ Press a key and a code races over USB to the CPU, into memory, and out to the screen.
→ In UTF-8, "नमस्ते" is six code points and eighteen bytes. Every script fits.
→ Every CPU loops three steps: fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it.
→ No multiply button? Add 7, six times, with a loop: 186 clock ticks.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/computerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a computer work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A computer is billions of switches following a list of tiny instructions, one clock tick at a time. Take a desktop apart, type your name and see its bytes, and step a real 8-bit CPU through fetch, decode and execute.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/computerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/computerclear

In this video:
• The same few parts. Every computer has a processor (CPU) that follows instructions, fast working memory (RAM) that forgets when the power goes off, storage (an SSD) that keeps your files, a graphics chip for the screen, and a power supply, all joined by a circuit board's buses.
• Everything is ones and zeros. A transistor is a switch: on is 1, off is 0.
• Fetch, decode, execute. A CPU loops three steps: fetch the next instruction from memory using the program counter, decode what it means, and execute it by steering data through the ALU and registers.
• Near and fast, far and slow. Registers answer at once, the L1 cache in about a nanosecond, RAM in about 100 ns, the SSD in tens of microseconds.
• Code becomes machine code. A compiler turns lines people can read into the numbered instructions a CPU runs.
• From a room to a pocket. ENIAC filled a room and added 5,000 numbers a second on 150 kW.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
